```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(splines)

load("data/MACS-VL.RData")
df <- macsVL
```



# question a

## overall variable conditions

```{r}
person <- df |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    vload = first(vload[!is.na(vload)], default = NA_real_),
    n_visits = n_distinct(month[!is.na(cd4) & !is.na(month)]),
    last_month = max(month, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```


```{r}
# baseline CD4
baseline <- df |>
  filter(month == 0) |>
  select(id, baseline_cd4 = cd4)

person <- person |>
  left_join(baseline, by = "id")


df |>
  summarise(
    n_participants = n_distinct(id),
    n_observations = n(),
    n_observed_cd4 = sum(!is.na(cd4))
  )
```


```{r}
summary_table <- person |>
  select(n_visits, last_month, vload, baseline_cd4) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(
    N = sum(!is.na(Value)),
    Missing = sum(is.na(Value)),
    Mean = mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1 = quantile(Value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q3 = quantile(Value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min = min(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max = max(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

summary_table
```



The dataset included 225 participants and 1,684 observations, with no missing CD4 values in the recorded observations. Participants had a median of 8 visits (IQR: 7–9), and the median last follow-up time was 45 months (IQR: 42–47). Baseline CD4 was available for 210 participants, with a median of 761 (IQR: 574.5–944). Baseline viral load was available for all participants and was right-skewed, with a mean of 78,347 and a median of 24,573 (IQR: 7,928–91,195).  


## baseline viral load


```{r}
# Extract one baseline viral load value per participant
person <- df |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    vload = first(vload[!is.na(vload)], default = NA_real_),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Check that all observed viral load values are positive
stopifnot(all(person$vload > 0, na.rm = TRUE))

# Calculate log10 viral load
person <- person |>
  mutate(log10_vload = log10(vload))

# Plot viral load distributions on the original and log10 scales
person |>
  select(vload, log10_vload) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Scale",
    values_to = "Viral_load"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Scale = factor(
      Scale,
      levels = c("vload", "log10_vload"),
      labels = c("Baseline viral load", "Log10 baseline viral load")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Viral_load)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 25,
    fill = "#4477AA",
    color = "white",
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of participants") +
  theme_minimal()
```



## speghatti plot

```{r}
# Define viral load groups using participant-level tertile cutoffs
vl_cutoffs <- quantile(
  person$vload,
  probs = c(1 / 3, 2 / 3),
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

person <- person |>
  mutate(
    vl_group = cut(
      vload,
      breaks = c(-Inf, vl_cutoffs, Inf),
      labels = c("Low viral load", "Middle viral load", "High viral load")
    )
  )

# Add viral load groups to the longitudinal data
df_plot <- df |>
  left_join(
    person |> select(id, vl_group),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(vl_group),
    !is.na(month),
    !is.na(cd4)
  ) |>
  arrange(id, month)

# Plot individual CD4 trajectories and group-specific smooth trends
ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = month, y = cd4)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(group = id),
    color = "grey60",
    alpha = 0.35,
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#CC6677",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ vl_group) +
  labs(
    x = "Months since baseline",
    y = "CD4 count",
    title = "CD4 trajectories by baseline viral load"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


Baseline viral load was strongly right-skewed, and the log10 transformation substantially reduced the skewness. CD4 counts generally declined over time in all three viral load groups, with considerable variation across individuals. The middle and high viral load groups showed greater overall declines than the low viral load group, suggesting a possible association between higher baseline viral load and faster CD4 decline.


# question b


```{r}
# Prepare complete observations for covariance exploration
df_cov <- df |>
  filter(
    !is.na(id),
    !is.na(month),
    !is.na(cd4),
    !is.na(vload),
    vload > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(log10_vload = log10(vload)) |>
  arrange(id, month)

# Fit a flexible mean model before examining covariance
mean_fit <- lm(
  cd4 ~ ns(month, df = 3) * log10_vload,
  data = df_cov
)

# Extract residuals without removing participant-specific differences
df_cov <- df_cov |>
  mutate(resid = residuals(mean_fit))
```


```{r}
# Group observations into approximately six-month windows
variance_summary <- df_cov |>
  mutate(time_window = 6 * floor(month / 6)) |>
  group_by(time_window) |>
  summarise(
    mean_month = mean(month),
    n_obs = n(),
    residual_variance = var(resid),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

variance_summary
```


```{r}
# Plot residual variance over follow-up time
ggplot(
  variance_summary,
  aes(x = mean_month, y = residual_variance)
) +
  geom_line(color = "#4477AA") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_obs), color = "#4477AA") +
  labs(
    x = "Months since baseline",
    y = "Residual variance",
    size = "Observations"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```


```{r}
# Construct all distinct within-participant observation pairs
pair_data <- df_cov |>
  group_by(id) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    if (nrow(.x) < 2) {
      return(tibble(lag = numeric(), semivariance = numeric()))
    }

    pair_index <- combn(seq_len(nrow(.x)), 2)
    j <- pair_index[1, ]
    k <- pair_index[2, ]

    tibble(
      lag = abs(.x$month[j] - .x$month[k]),
      semivariance = 0.5 * (.x$resid[j] - .x$resid[k])^2
    )
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(lag > 0)

# Average semivariances within six-month lag intervals
variogram_summary <- pair_data |>
  mutate(lag_window = 6 * floor(lag / 6)) |>
  group_by(lag_window) |>
  summarise(
    mean_lag = mean(lag),
    semivariance = mean(semivariance),
    n_pairs = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

variogram_summary
```


```{r}
# Plot the empirical variogram
ggplot(
  variogram_summary,
  aes(x = mean_lag, y = semivariance)
) +
  geom_line(color = "#CC6677") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_pairs), color = "#CC6677") +
  labs(
    x = "Time lag (months)",
    y = "Semivariance",
    size = "Observation pairs"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```


After adjusting for the mean trajectory and baseline viral load, residual variance varied across follow-up periods without a clear monotonic trend. The estimate at month 48 was based on only 38 observations and should be interpreted cautiously. The empirical variogram generally increased with time lag, suggesting weaker within-participant correlation between measurements taken farther apart, although changing variances may also contribute to this pattern.

A continuous-time AR(1), or exponential correlation structure, is therefore a reasonable candidate given the irregular observation times. Compound symmetry appears less suitable because it assumes constant correlation across time lags. Models allowing time-varying variances could also be considered.
